Triggers.value: Medical equipment such as needles or drips

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try to erase the memory of the event
constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy

Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

Negative Appraisals.value: My life has been destroyed by the trauma
I have failed in my most important role in life
My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

issues.item: Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
issues.explanation: 'Being in nature similar to where it happened' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of life-threatening illness, which typically involves medical/health contexts rather than a natural-environment trauma setting.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
issues.explanation: 'Avoid grief reminders' implies bereavement/loss of another person, which does not fit the stated trauma type of life-threatening illness unless there is an unreported death-related trauma; it is not supported by the other selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: 'Fear of rage' is weakly connected to the rest of the profile: the other appraisals and memory items center on damage, unreality, and role failure after illness, not anger-based dyscontrol. This makes the appraisal set less internally coherent.

vignette:
Linh Tran is a 42-year-old Vietnamese American woman who works as a project manager for a mid-sized construction firm in Houston. She is married with two school-aged children and, until approximately eighteen months ago, had built what she described in her intake session as "a very controlled life" - detailed schedules, colour-coded calendars, a reputation at work for never missing a deadline. That sense of control collapsed in the winter of the previous year, when what she had dismissed as persistent fatigue and a low-grade fever was diagnosed, within the space of seventy-two hours, as bacterial meningitis. She was admitted to the ICU in a state of rapid deterioration, and for several days her survival was genuinely uncertain.

What Linh remembers of those days is fractured in a way she finds deeply unsettling. Certain moments are engraved with terrible precision: the particular antiseptic smell of the ICU that seemed to coat the back of her throat, the sensation of cold - the room, the IV fluids running into her arm, the metal rail of the bed - and the sight of the drip line snaking from the bag above her to the needle taped at the crook of her elbow. These details return to her with a vividness she cannot account for, while the hours around them are entirely blank. She cannot remember her husband's face during that time. She cannot remember whether she was frightened. What she finds perhaps most disorienting is that the memory, in its totality, carries a quality of unreality - it is so extreme, she has told her therapist, that she cannot fully accept it as something that happened to her specifically, to Linh, in her own body. Yet without any warning or clear image to anchor it, she will sometimes be overtaken by the full emotional weight of that period: a wave of terror and helplessness that arrives without a picture attached to it, leaving her shaking and unable to identify its source.

In the months following her discharge, these experiences began to organise themselves around her daily life in ways that narrowed it considerably. The smell of hospital-grade disinfectant - encountered once in the cleaning supply aisle of a grocery store - sent her out of the building immediately. She began routing her commute to avoid the street on which the hospital sat. When her firm scheduled a site visit that required her to walk through a section of a building where the ventilation was poor and the air held a faint chemical chill, she fabricated a scheduling conflict rather than attend. Her avoidance of anything medically adjacent became comprehensive: she has not attended a routine physical examination since her discharge, has declined to accompany her children to their paediatric appointments, and changes the channel or leaves the room when hospital dramas appear on television. Her husband has noticed, though Linh has not fully explained why, that she flinches when she opens the refrigerator too quickly and the cold air reaches her face.

Linh has come to believe, with a quiet but absolute conviction, that her body is no longer trustworthy - that the illness revealed a fundamental fragility in her that cannot be reversed. She is certain that the damage done during those days in the ICU is permanent in ways that have not yet been fully measured. Alongside this sits a belief she finds shameful to articulate: that she has failed as a mother. She was hospitalised during a school performance. Her children saw her unconscious. She had been, in her own understanding, the person responsible for holding her family together, and she had instead become the emergency. She monitors her own thoughts with vigilance, watching for signs that her mind is becoming unstable, interpreting moments of confusion or emotional flooding as evidence that something is wrong with her neurologically. She tries, with considerable effort, to simply not think about the hospitalisation - to overwrite it, to fill the space it occupies with work tasks and logistics - though she acknowledges this has not succeeded.

What finally brought Linh to seek help was a performance review at work in which her supervisor noted, gently but formally, that her project documentation had become inconsistent and that she had missed two client calls without explanation. For a woman whose professional identity had been built on precision, this was intolerable. She arrived at her first session composed and businesslike, but when asked what she was hoping for, she was quiet for a long moment before saying that she wanted to feel like herself again - and then, more quietly, that she was afraid that version of herself no longer existed.
